# Building .dot apps on the Polkadot Products Devnet — notes for an LLM

You are probably here because you are writing or debugging an app that runs inside the
Polkadot app (the "shell"), published to a `.dot` name. This file is the shortest path
between "it does nothing and there is no error" and working code.

Everything below was established by building, publishing and operating seven apps on the
devnet between 2026-07-23 and 2026-07-27, and re-verified against the live chain. The
same ground stated as a report for the platform's engineers is in `DEVFEEDBACK.md`;
this file is the practical half. Where a claim is unverified, it says so.

**The one rule that matters:** on this platform, *the normal failure mode is silence*.
The most expensive bug in this file was a permission nobody told us to ask for (T0).
Blocked fetches, blocked popups, wedged host calls and clipped tooltips all present as
"the button does nothing". Assume nothing worked until you have evidence it did, and
never write a code path whose failure is invisible.

---

## 1. Verified constants

```
EVM RPC (public, no key)   https://paseo-assethub-rpc.laissez-faire.trade
Substrate RPC             wss://asset-hub-paseo-rpc.n.dwellir.com
DotNS registry            0x527b08a640b527a3dae0C4BE04D7344E430B6E50
Content resolver          0x326bdE29315199c814B1c58b431D84D16EA5cE41   <- call this directly
Browse (official listing)  0xaab42efbe8ea4d4228c3a11e973f94c17b9a0f2c
Personhood precompile     0x000000000000000000000000000000000a010000
App iframe sandbox (web gateway, read from the live DOM):
  allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms allow-pointer-lock allow-popups
  (no allow-downloads, no allow-top-navigation)
```

Shell page is `<name>.dev-dot.li`; the app itself runs in a cross-origin iframe at
`<name>.app.dev-dot.li/?chainBackend=…&cid=…`.

---

## 2. The traps

### T0 — Ask for the permission the API you are calling never mentions

**Read this before anything else.** It is the trap that cost the most, and the
cheapest to avoid.

**Symptom:** an SDK call does nothing on one shell and works on another. Most often:
external links open on desktop and are dead on mobile.

**Cause:** capabilities are gated by **device permissions**, and the API that uses them
does not say so. The full set:

```ts
type HostDevicePermissionRequest =
  | 'Notifications' | 'Camera' | 'Microphone' | 'Bluetooth' | 'NFC'
  | 'Location' | 'Clipboard' | 'OpenUrl' | 'Biometrics';
```

`OpenUrl` gates **leaving the app for a link** — the thing `navigateTo` does — and
`navigateTo`'s own documentation never mentions it. `Clipboard` gates the copy button
you probably built as your fallback, so a missing permission can take out the escape
hatch and the escape hatch's escape hatch at once. Some shells grant these implicitly
(the web one appears to), which is exactly what makes the bug so expensive: it works
everywhere you test until it silently does not.

**Fix:** request them at startup, next to your network origins, and again lazily before
first use.

```ts
await host.requestPermission({ tag: 'Remote', value: { domains: ORIGINS } });
for (const kind of ['OpenUrl', 'Clipboard'] as const) {
  await host.requestDevicePermission(kind).catch(() => undefined);
}
```

Two rules that are not obvious:

- **Bound them.** A permission request is a host call and can hang like any other (T1).
  Race it; never let app startup depend on one resolving.
- **A failed *request* is not a *denial*.** On a host that does not implement a
  permission, the request itself errors. If you treat that as "denied" and refuse to
  act, you have written a new bug on top of the platform's. Default to attempting the
  action, and record which happened.

**General principle for this platform:** when a capability is silently unavailable, ask
whether it has a name in `HostDevicePermissionRequest` before concluding the platform is
broken. Camera, microphone, location, clipboard, notifications, biometrics, NFC,
Bluetooth and opening a URL are all gated. Nothing warns you.

### T1 — Host calls can hang forever, so your fallback never runs

**Symptom:** a button that calls the SDK does nothing, with no error and no console output.

**Cause:** the TrUAPI client has **no request timeout**, and its iframe transport queues
frames while the channel to the host is not established (`@parity/truapi/dist/sandbox.js`,
`postMessage` pushes to `queued` with no timer). `await navigateTo(url)` can therefore
never settle. Any fallback written after that `await` is unreachable code.

**Fix:** race every host call against a deadline. Never `await` a host call bare.

```ts
const outcome = await Promise.race([
  host.navigateTo(url).then((r) => (r.ok ? 'ok' : 'refused')),
  new Promise<'timeout'>((res) => setTimeout(() => res('timeout'), 1500)),
]);
```

Also: `isInsideContainer()` is **not** a health check — it resolves `window !== window.top`.
Use it to choose an order, never to skip a fallback. Prefer the sync
`isInsideContainerSync()`; the async one only wraps it and adds a failure point.

### T2 — `window.open(url, '_blank', 'noopener')` returns null even when it works

**Symptom:** you check the return value, always get `null`, and conclude popups are blocked.

**Cause:** per spec, the `noopener` feature makes `window.open` return `null`. Success and
blockage become indistinguishable.

**Fix:** drop the feature and sever the opener on the handle.

```ts
const w = window.open(url, '_blank');
if (w) { try { w.opener = null; } catch {} }
```

### T3 — When the mobile shell still will not open a link

**Symptom:** external links work in the desktop shell and do nothing in the mobile app,
from the same published bundle.

**First check T0** — the `OpenUrl` permission is the likely cause and the cheap fix.
What follows is the belt-and-braces layer for when a shell refuses anyway.

**Cause:** `navigateTo` does not answer (T1) and `window.open` produces no visible window.

**Fix:** hand the URL to the operating system instead. Mobile web views honour platform
schemes even when they refuse popups. Use a detached iframe, not `location.href`: an
unclaimed scheme then fails silently instead of stranding the app on an error page.

```ts
const url = isIOS()
  ? `maps://?q=${encodeURIComponent(name)}&ll=${lat},${lon}`
  : `geo:${lat},${lon}?q=${lat},${lon}(${encodeURIComponent(name)})`;
const f = document.createElement('iframe');
f.style.cssText = 'position:absolute;width:0;height:0;border:0;visibility:hidden';
f.src = url;
document.body.appendChild(f);
setTimeout(() => f.remove(), 1500);
```

A scheme handoff returns **no signal**. Never report success from it — keep a visible
"didn't open? here is the link" affordance either way.

**Practical strategy that survives all three engines:** try the host (raced), then the
popup, then a sheet showing the URL with a copy button and a real `<a>` the *user* taps.
Remember in `sessionStorage` that the host did not answer, and skip it on later taps —
a popup is only allowed while the tap is still "transiently active", and waiting on a
wedged host spends exactly that window. Keep a breadcrumb (`host:timeout>popup:blocked>manual`)
and show it: it converts "it does nothing" into a diagnosis.

### T4 — Ignoring the History API turns the back gesture into "quit"

**Symptom:** a back swipe exits the app instead of returning to the previous view. Or
worse: the first swipe appears to do nothing and the second closes the app.

**Cause:** the shell pops history. An app that navigates by internal state pushes nothing,
so there is nothing to pop. An app that pushes (e.g. by setting `location.hash`) but does
not listen for `popstate`/`hashchange` rewinds the URL while the view stays put.

**Fix:** push on navigate, and *follow* the URL back.

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  const sync = () => setView(parse(window.location.hash));
  addEventListener('hashchange', sync);
  addEventListener('popstate', sync);
  return () => { removeEventListener('hashchange', sync); removeEventListener('popstate', sync); };
}, []);
```
In-app back buttons should call `history.back()`, not push another entry.

### T5 — Outbound fetches fail silently until you ask for the origin

**Symptom:** `fetch()` fails exactly like a network error; controls appear inert.

**Fix:** request every origin **once, at startup**, as hostnames (not URLs).

```ts
await host.requestPermission({ tag: 'Remote', value: { domains: ['nominatim.openstreetmap.org', 'tile.openstreetmap.org'] } });
```

### T6 — A nested third-party iframe blanks the whole app

No console output, no error. Do not embed iframes (map embeds, widgets). For maps, use
raw tile `<img>` elements; they load fine once the tile host is permitted (T5).

### T7 — Native `<select>` did not open on tested devices

Replace every `<select>` with a custom control: chips, a segmented control, a bottom sheet,
or a range input. (Not fully isolated to the shell — but the workaround costs an hour and
removes the question.)

### T8 — `registry.resolver(node)` points at a resolver that reverts

**Symptom:** `text()` / `contenthash()` revert; you conclude records are unreadable and
start reading raw storage slots.

**Cause:** the registry's resolver pointer returns a dead address for most names (36 of 66
checked; 8 point at the working resolver, `browse.dot` among them; 22 have no record).

**Fix:** ignore the pointer and call the content resolver directly at
`0x326bdE29315199c814B1c58b431D84D16EA5cE41`. `text(node,'manifest')`,
`contenthash(node)` and `text(namehash('app.'+label+'.dot'),'executable')` all work over
plain `eth_call`, no host and no personhood required.

The gallery manifest is a text record named `manifest`:

```json
{"$v":1,"displayName":"…","description":"…","icon":{"cid":"baf…","format":"png"}}
```

This is also your only "SEO": it is the sole machine-readable description of an app.
14 of 42 registered names have one. If you publish an app, write it.

**If your app has a contract, publish its address too:**

```bash
dotns text set <name>.dot contract 0xYourContract --env devnet
```

There is no official field for this (see `DEVFEEDBACK.md` #8) — it is a convention
dotmetrics reads, because without a name→contract mapping the only per-app metrics
possible are ones whose ABI the index author hand-coded, which in practice means the
index author's own apps. Event counts per address need no ABI, so a published address is
enough to be measured on the same footing as everyone else.

**Design note worth stealing:** if you build anything that ranks apps, check whether your
top tier is reachable by apps other than your own. Ours was not, at first: "live data"
required a reader we had written, and we had only written ours. Disclosure did not fix
it — changing the ranking to use only universally measurable facts did.

### T9 — Labels scraped from calldata are ~1/3 garbage

**Symptom:** your index lists names that do not exist.

**Cause:** registry events carry only hashed names, so enumeration means walking blocks and
extracting ascii runs from raw registration calldata. That admits noise.

**Fix:** verify every candidate before admitting it.

```
registry.owner(namehash(label + '.dot')) != 0x0
```
On our data this removed 21 of 63 candidates. Also: any `lastSeenBlock`-style field derived
from that scan is meaningless — never build a metric on it.

### T10 — Every write is personhood-gated, and you probably do not have it

`press()`, `sign()`, `review()`, `book()` revert with `NotHuman(0, …)` for an ordinary
devnet account. Design **demo-first**: a fully usable local/demo path, with the real
contract deployed and *read* live behind it, and a single flag to switch the demo off.
Reads are permissionless — use them, they are what makes the demo honest.

Names shorter than 9 characters additionally require **Full** personhood to register, and
the CLI only tells you *after* the commit transaction.

### T11 — `pad` / `dotns` output is unusable in scripts

The progress spinner emits one character per line in non-TTY captures. The stable lines
are `Incremental: previous contenthash…`, `Setting contenthash:`, `Verified on-chain:`.
For a CID, grep the raw output:

```bash
CID=$(dotns bulletin upload file.json --env devnet 2>&1 | tr -d '\r' | grep -aoE 'baf[a-z0-9]{50,}' | head -1)
```
Always gate a publish on `Verified on-chain` actually appearing, or a failed publish looks
like a successful one.

### T12 — Build on the OS that owns `node_modules`

If `node_modules` was installed on Windows, a WSL build fails on missing native binaries —
and a scheduled job that ignores the failure will happily republish the *old* `dist` and
report success. From WSL, build through interop and abort on failure:

```bash
cmd.exe /c "npm run build" || { echo "build failed — not publishing"; exit 1; }
```

### T13 — `touch-action: none` eats the shell's gestures

Set on a chart or canvas so pointer tracking works, it swallows every swipe that begins
there — including the shell's back gesture. Use `touch-action: pan-y`. Likewise
`overscroll-behavior: none` on the document disables gestures app-wide.

### T14 — Fixed-width SVG is clipped on a phone

A chart with `width={800}` inside a 342px container hides its right-hand side, and a
horizontal scroller for it fights the shell's swipe. Use `width="100%"` with a `viewBox`
and cap it with `style={{ maxWidth: NATURAL_W }}`. Derive any pointer maths from the
*rendered* width: `scale = rect.width / VIEWBOX_W`.

### T15 — Tooltips get clipped by their own card

Cards clip overflow, so a tip above the top row and a tip below the bottom row both leave
the card. Choose the side from the available space, and pin to the left/right edge near
the sides.

### T16 — Historical blocks do not decode; custom signed extensions break vanilla tooling

Decoding old extrinsics via `@polkadot/api` fails with `findMetaCall: Unable to find Call
with index` after a runtime upgrade — use **events** plus raw block bytes. And transactions
built with vanilla polkadot.js/PAPI fail against this chain's signed-extension set
(`AsPgas`, `AsPerson`, …): sign through the Product SDK.

### T17 — Nothing indexes .dot apps, including the official directory

Browse holds 19 entries storing only labelhashes, emits zero logs, and `labelOf()` returns
empty — 4 of 19 names are recoverable by brute force. The web gateway serves a byte-identical
shell for every name, so no web crawler sees any app. If discoverability matters to your
app, you cannot rely on being found: write your `manifest` record (T8) and expect to be
indexed only by someone walking the chain.

### T18 — "Self-updating" needs a cron outside the platform

Bulletin hosting is static and there is no platform-native scheduled compute. A site that
refreshes its own data needs an external runner (GitHub Actions works; free tier is enough)
and therefore a publish key in a secret store. Budget for that, and never put a key with
real value in it.

### T19 — Your published site expires. So does your permission to renew it

**This one is silent, delayed, and total.** Nothing fails at publish time; the site simply
stops existing a fortnight later, most likely on the day someone finally clicks your link.

**Cause:** storage is a *retention window*, not permanence. Parity's write-up on Levity —
the layer Bulletin belongs to — states the window is "approximately fourteen days" and
that without renewal data "falls off the network automatically". Renewal means publishing
again; there is no renew verb in the CLI. Separately, your **write authorization** has its
own expiry, and when it lapses you can neither publish nor renew:

```bash
dotns bulletin status --env devnet --json
# {"authorized":true,"expired":false,"transactions":200,"bytes":"59768832",
#  "expiresAt":"2026-08-07T00:27:13.488Z"}
```

**Fix:** a scheduled republish at **half the retention window or less**, so one failed run
cannot expire anything, plus a check that reports how many days of authorization remain
before it becomes urgent. `pad` is incremental, so republishing unchanged files is cheap.
An app that already refreshes its own data on a schedule renews itself for free — the ones
that need this are the finished, stable apps nobody has touched in a while, which is
exactly the set you would never think to check.

**Also verify where your content is actually reachable.** `dotns bulletin verify <cid>`
checks a CID across gateways, and the honest answer today can be one gateway out of four:

```
✓ https://devnet-ipfs.api.polkadotcommunity.foundation/ipfs
✗ https://dweb.link   ✗ https://cloudflare-ipfs.com   ✗ https://w3s.link
```

If your app fetches its own data by CID through a public gateway (a common pattern for
mutable data), test the gateway you chose rather than assuming IPFS-compatible means
IPFS-reachable.

---

## 3. Checklist before you ship

- [ ] `OpenUrl` and `Clipboard` device permissions requested at startup (T0)
- [ ] Every host call raced against a deadline; no bare `await` on the SDK
- [ ] Every external link has a visible fallback that cannot fail (copy the URL)
- [ ] Views push history; `popstate`/`hashchange` restore them
- [ ] All outbound origins requested at startup, as hostnames
- [ ] No `<select>`, no nested iframes, no `touch-action: none` on large surfaces
- [ ] Charts responsive by `viewBox`, tooltips side-aware
- [ ] Write paths gated → demo path that works for everyone, with reads live from chain
- [ ] `manifest` text record written, icon uploaded to Bulletin
- [ ] Publish gated on `Verified on-chain`
- [ ] A scheduled republish exists, at half the retention window or less (T19)
- [ ] Failure states say what failed, in words a non-developer can repeat back to you

## 4. If you are debugging "it does nothing"

1. Is the capability permission-gated? Check T0 first — `OpenUrl`, `Clipboard`, Camera,
   Location and five others are gated, and the APIs that use them do not say so.
   Then T1 (hang), T2 (null handle), T5 (network origins).
2. Reproduce **inside the shell**, not just locally: load `https://<name>.dev-dot.li`, and
   read the app iframe's `sandbox` attribute from the parent page. Desktop and mobile
   shells behave differently — a fix verified on desktop proves nothing about mobile.
3. Verify what is actually published: compare the on-chain contenthash
   (`dotns content view <name>.dot --env devnet`) with your local build. Vite's asset
   filenames are content hashes — same name means same bytes.
4. Instrument before you guess. A breadcrumb string in the UI turned three wrong theories
   into one measurement, in the work that produced this file.
